newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zairean rebels seen eager to draw foreign miners.
newsitem.headline: Zairean rebels seen eager to draw foreign miners.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila, poised to take full control of the country's vast untapped mineral wealth, is likely to welcome foreign mining companies, analysts and industry officials said on Tuesday.
Kabila's rebels were nearing the copper and cobalt mining centre of Lubumbashi in Shaba province which would give them complete control of Zaire's mineral industry.
The rebels, who took up arms against President Mobutu Sese Seko in October, already control more than a third of Zaire -- including the diamond and gold producing areas.
"Kabila is no one's fool, he knows that the longer term survival of Zaire depends on the short term impact he makes on the outside world," BOE Natwest mining analyst Barry Sergeant said.
"The quickest way he could make an impact, is by giving Western (mining) companies a signal that they are not only welcome there but their investments...will be safe."
Zaire is viewed as potentially one of the richest mineral areas in the world yet to be fully explored.

Despite growing political and economic chaos, the country was Africa's fifth largest mineral producer in 1995. Its $1.5 billion worth of mineral exports in 1995 put it behind South Africa, Gabon, Guinea and Zimbabwe.

Many of the world's largest mining companies are watching events in Zaire closely and some, like Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd and De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd have already held talks with Kabila.

De Beers spokesman Tom Tweedy said the company's interests in Zaire fell in territory now under Kabila's control. "We were concerned about those properties and so we went to just go and express our concerns and he noted them," Tweedy said.

Until recently De Beers had five diamond buying offices in Zaire and a contract with MIBA (Societe Miniere de Bakwanga) to buy its production. But it pulled staff out of Kisangani in December and from the diamond capital Mbuji-Mayi, now in rebel hands, a few weeks ago.
Tweedy said De Beers would return to Zaire when civil order was restored.
Sergeant and E.W Balderson metals analyst Stephen Briggs said they believed that Kabila -- who comes from Shaba -- would be realistic and encourage foreign mining companies to invest.
"It can't be worse than under Mobutu," Briggs said.
Sergeant said the possible pay-offs in Zaire were so great that Western mining companies would be willing to take risks.
"The potential rewards are so enormous that any company which can afford to be involved in Zaire has to be there," he said.
Sergeant cited the Tenke Fungurume copper-cobalt mine in Shaba for which Canada's Tenke Mining Corp won mining rights from Zaire's state mining concern Gecamines.
The mine could be one of the lowest cost producers in the world -- with much of the ore contained in hilltops.
"The trucks go up empty and then they drive down with gravity behind them when they are fully loaded. It is a project from heaven," Sergeant said.
The mine has potential reserves of 222 million tonnes of ore of which an average 4.4 percent will become pure copper and 0.33 percent cobalt.
